Whereas it is the duty of all Nations to acknowledge the providence of Almighty God, to obey his will, to be grateful for his benefits, and humbly to implore his protection and favor— and whereas both Houses of Congress have by their joint Committee requested me to ‘recommend to the People of the United States a day of public thanksgiving and prayer to be observed by acknowledging with grateful hearts the many signal favors of Almighty God especially by affording them an opportunity peaceably to establish a form of government for their safety and happiness.’

Therefore, I do recommend and assign Thursday the 26th day of November next to be devoted by the People of these States to the service of that great and glorious Being, who is the beneficent Author of all the good that was, that is, or that will be.

May we all unite in rendering unto him our sincere and humble thanks— for his kind care and protection of the People of this Country previous to their becoming a Nation— for the signal and manifold mercies, and the favorable interpositions of his Providence which we experienced in the course and conclusion of the late war— for the great degree of tranquillity, union, and plenty, which we have since enjoyed— for the peaceable and rational manner, in which we have been enabled to establish constitutions of government for our safety and happiness, and particularly the national One now lately instituted— for the civil and religious liberty with which we are blessed; and the means we have of acquiring and diffusing useful knowledge; and in general for all the great and various favors which he hath been pleased to confer upon us.

And also that we may then unite in most humbly offering our prayers and supplications to the great Lord and Ruler of Nations to render our national government a blessing to all the people, by constantly being a Government of wise, just, and constitutional laws, discreetly and faithfully executed and obeyed— to promote the knowledge and practice of true religion and virtue, and the encrease of science among them and us— and generally to grant unto all Mankind such a degree of temporal prosperity as he alone knows to be best.

Under my hand at the City of New-York, 3rd of October in the year of our Lord 1789."

Inflationary is intensifying in Japan:

Japan’s Services Producer Price Index (SPPI) jumped +4.2% YoY in October, its largest annual increase since 1990, and far above expectations of +3.6%.

This index tracks domestic prices businesses charge each other for services, and serves as a key inflation metric in Japan.

MoM, the index rose +1.1%, up from +0.3% in the previous month and marking its biggest monthly increase in 6 months.

The latest surge was driven particularly by higher ocean freight transportation costs, leasing costs, and hotel charges.

Prices in transport and postal activities alone jumped +9.4% YoY in October, following an +8.4% increase in September.

Rising inflationary pressures are strengthening the case for a December rate hike by the Bank of Japan.

This index tracks domestic prices businesses charge each other for services, and serves as a key inflation metric in Japan.

MoM, the index rose +1.1%, up from +0.3% in the previous month and marking its biggest monthly increase in 6 months.

The latest surge was driven particularly by higher ocean freight transportation costs, leasing costs, and hotel charges.

Prices in transport and postal activities alone jumped +9.4% YoY in October, following an +8.4% increase in September.

Rising inflationary pressures are strengthening the case for a December rate hike by the Bank of Japan.

1. Asian neoclouds (eg. Malaysia/Thailand) had their deals cancelled with Bytedance, Tencent etc. due to US export controls.

This is more nuanced, it means less compute/competition comes online in the future, which is a good thing for players like $NBIS?

There's still the overall macro risks like rate hikes, financing, etc. where Neoclouds are typically the most impacted

Too many multifaceted variables at play here; but I think Weebius is the best and ends up on top

$HGRAF $HG.CN #Graphene #Cement

How much of the world’s cement would have to contain HydroGraph graphene for the stock to go 100×? Using the assumptions in my table below, I get just under 3%. That gives plastics, coatings, batteries and defense a combined value of zero.

The number worth revisiting is US$250/kg. CEO Kjirstin Breure has discussed that low end of pricing for large bulk orders of HydroGraph’s fractal graphene. Cement is exactly where I’d use it. A precast producer buying the same additive by the tonne has every reason to negotiate the best bulk price. A customer buying a specialty formulation with HydroGraph’s IP is a different sale.

So why would a concrete producer pay even US$250/kg? At a dosage tested by Arizona State researchers, one tonne of cement takes just 200 grams of graphene. That’s US$50. Lab tests on mortar showed early compressive strength gains of up to 70%. For a precast plant, the question is whether getting a beam out of its mold sooner lets it cast more beams per week. That’s a benefit a plant manager can put a dollar figure on.

Now take that 200-gram dose to a market that produced 3.8 BILLION tonnes of cement in 2025. If HydroGraph supplied the graphene going into 3% of that output, the annual numbers would be:

• 114 million tonnes of cement treated
• 22,800 tonnes of dry graphene sold
• US$5.7 billion in revenue at US$250/kg
• Just under US$3 billion in earnings at my modeled 52.5% net margin

My original 20,000-tonne row worked out to C$362.25/share at 40× earnings. Extend that same row to 22,800 tonnes, keep the same 400 million diluted shares and exchange rate, and I get C$413/share. Against the November 25 close of C$4.00, that’s roughly 103×.

Why I keep a potential 100× outcome on the table for HydroGraph and have made it my biggest bet ever: exceptional margins combined with production capacity that can be replicated.

The attached table puts numbers behind that possibility.

At an assumed selling price of US$250/kg, selling 10,000 tonnes annually would generate US$2.5 BILLION in revenue. US$250/kg is the minimum price, in most cases it will be much higher.

Start with an assumed 80% gross margin. Deduct operating expenses equal to 10% of revenue, then apply 25% tax. That leaves a 52.5% net margin and approximately US$1.31 billion in annual earnings.

• 5,000 tonnes at P/E 30 → C$67.92/share. • 10,000 tonnes at P/E 30 → C$135.84/share. • 20,000 tonnes at P/E 40 → C$362.25/share.

These are conditional future valuations, not price targets. The assumptions are shown in the table.

Its modular Hyperion reactors can be built in months. If commercial margins hold and customers place repeat orders, profits could help fund additional reactors and eventually additional sites.

That creates a compelling possibility: growing volumes, strong earnings and expansion increasingly funded internally.

The opportunity spans coatings, polymers, concrete and defense. Successful adoption across several of those markets could support a business far larger than the first Texas facility.

My opinion. Not financial advice. Do your own DD.

If you bought $10,000 of Bitcoin at the October 2025 top, it's worth about $4,900 today.

• The good news is we're in the same zone where the last 3 bottoms formed.
• The bad news is there might be one more 13% drop first.

Here are the 5 signals I'm watching:

1. Coins in profit: bullish

On November 20, only about 43% of all Bitcoin was worth more than what people paid for it.

That's lower than right after the 2022 bottom.

This number has been under 45% on about 150 days in Bitcoin's history. A year later, BTC was higher every time.

2. Realized price: bearish

Realized price is about what the average holder paid for their BTC. Right now that's about $53.3K, and BTC is around $61.2K.

At the last 3 bottoms, BTC fell to that price or lower before it turned around. It hasn't done that yet.

So my two favorite signals disagree, and honestly I don't know which one wins this time.

3. Long-term holders selling at a loss: bearish for now

On November 20, people who held for a long time sold their coins for about 36% less than they paid.

This kind of selling can go on for weeks. I want to see the losses get smaller while the price holds.

4. ETF flows: bearish

For me this is the big one.

People have pulled about $5.4B out of US Bitcoin ETFs so far in November. That's already the worst month since these funds launched.

Def a leading indicator to pay attention to.

5. Miners: just starting to hurt

The average miner is losing money right now. Earlier this year it cost them about $75K to make 1 BTC, and BTC is around $61.2K.

The total power miners use is down about 7% from a year ago, and a signal called the Hash Ribbon just flipped. It flips when miners start shutting off machines.

The last time it flipped was late November 2025. It took about 3 months for miners to bounce back, and at past bottoms, that bounce back was the real buy signal.

There's a twist this time though. A lot of big miners are moving their power to AI data centers because it pays more.

Some of these machines are getting shut off for a better business, so I trust this signal a bit less than before.

So, is the bottom in?

I think this is a good area to start buying slowly. I just wouldn't call it the bottom yet.

Buying a little now and keeping some cash works either way. If this is the bottom, you're in. If it drops more, you can buy more.

Before I'd buy bigger, I want to see:

• BTC holding $55K to $60K
• Long-term holders selling at smaller losses
• Money coming back into the ETFs
• Miners starting to recover

Do you think Bitcoin has already bottomed, or is there one more drop coming?

At the last 3 bottoms, BTC fell to that price or lower before it turned around. It hasn't done that yet.

So my two favorite signals disagree, and honestly I don't know which one wins this time.

3. Long-term holders selling at a loss: bearish for now

On November 20, people who held for a long time sold their coins for about 36% less than they paid.

This kind of selling can go on for weeks. I want to see the losses get smaller while the price holds.

4. ETF flows: bearish

For me this is the big one.

People have pulled about $5.4B out of US Bitcoin ETFs so far in November. That's already the worst month since these funds launched.

Def a leading indicator to pay attention to.

5. Miners: just starting to hurt

The average miner is losing money right now. Earlier this year it cost them about $75K to make 1 BTC, and BTC is around $61.2K.

The total power miners use is down about 7% from a year ago, and a signal called the Hash Ribbon just flipped. It flips when miners start shutting off machines.

The last time it flipped was late November 2025. It took about 3 months for miners to bounce back, and at past bottoms, that bounce back was the real buy signal.

There's a twist this time though. A lot of big miners are moving their power to AI data centers because it pays more.

Some of these machines are getting shut off for a better business, so I trust this signal a bit less than before.

So, is the bottom in?

I think this is a good area to start buying slowly. I just wouldn't call it the bottom yet.

Buying a little now and keeping some cash works either way. If this is the bottom, you're in. If it drops more, you can buy more.

Before I'd buy bigger, I want to see:

• BTC holding $55K to $60K
• Long-term holders selling at smaller losses
• Money coming back into the ETFs
• Miners starting to recover

Do you think Bitcoin has already bottomed, or is there one more drop coming?

I think 2026 has been one of the most challenging years to navigate equities over the past four years.

Let's walk through how this year started and all of the things one needed to do in order to actually participate in the bull market...

To start off, I think 2026 was fundamentally different from 2023, 2024, and 2025 because of sector rotation and long/short pair trades across different sectors. 

Over the past 3 years, everyone lost money together across all industries when the markets went down and everyone made money when everything went up. The trend was quite literally your friend and if you followed it short, you won, if you followed it long, you won. 

2026 was different.

First, in January you had to basically get two trades right to really benefit: long oil and long metals. We saw gold and silver breakout of a 15 year base and we saw a Venezuela operation that made oil the most important commodity trade of the year. However, you then had to sell commodities into a blow off top by the end of January. If you didn't, you had a 40% drawdown waiting for you. 

As we got into the end of February, we saw the administration take us into a war. No one knew how long it really would last for as it was pitched as a short, special operation. It ended up taking the S&P down to 6200 and growth stocks were down 30-40%. Once again, you had to really be long oil or short the $QQQ to seriously benefit off of this.

So, let's say you bought the dip coming out of March and into April when the first ceasefire was announced. We essentially got the most aggressive, leveraged rally we had seen in a decade from March to June...but only in semis. 

If you didn't own the semis, you really didn't benefit. You also couldn't just own anything in $SMH, you had to own very high-beta semiconductor stocks that were the definition of picks and shovels, essentially the bottleneck bros trade. Owning $NVDA was not going to carry your year even though it was the most important semiconductor company. Now, you could have also participated in some other sectors, like space with names like $RKLB $RDW $ASTS, but you had to be aggressively in something within the most high-beta growth sectors for the market to feel comfortable giving you a premium. 

If you owned anything in software, you had to suffer 50-60% declines across some of the most incredible companies in the space like $PLTR, $SHOP, and $MSFT because the narrative became that Anthropic would kill software. $IGV got cut by 30%. 

Well, then comes July. Now, we finally figured out why software was getting hit as hard as it did. Leopold had made one trade very popular -- long semis, short software. Other hedgefunds had copied it. The problem was, the trade had become so popular and so leveraged that other market participants realized a collapse of the trade could literally wipe out entire funds and the overall sectors. As much money as was made on the upside for the AI trade, the downside had now begun. Leopold's fund blew up but survived, Citadel came in and bought everything at a steep discount, and AI names basically fell 50-60%. 

In August, we got a bounce. If the entire downside of the trade was based on a hedgefund getting over levered, then that meant the AI trade was back on since the main event had already taken place. However, things felt different. The excitement around memory had faded. The neoclouds were not seeing the same momentum as they were before. AI names were still doing well, but something obviously fell off. If you did not sell the June highs and chose to hold on, you were basically getting ready to roundtrip the entire gains as we progressed through the year. The space names literally fell 70% as $SPCX marked the top for the market and for the space names. 

The reason this is so important is because I believe many people bought most of these AI names in May/June, not early in the year. I am a victim of that as well. The rally was so aggressive that if you didn't have any meaningful semi exposure, you probably ended up buying something that was more rooted in hype even if the fundamentals were strong. I mean some of these names were flat for 25 years and had just seen a massive move up, so obviously there were a ton of people buying into names that likely were too high to begin with. 

Towards the end of August, the software trade finally started coming back, along with the hyperscalers. $META began showing off Muse, $MSFT guided to FCF positive, $AMZN had their best operating margins ever. Apple $AAPL was strong all year as a defensive play. The narrative about Claude destroying software went away. 

September was flat. Nothing crazy to see.

Then came October. We hit ATHs again, not every name in the AI trade got to their June highs, but many names came back. $NBIS was back to $250, $NVDA hit $240, it felt like the bull market was back in action. 

Unfortunately, $CRWV was the reason everything changed. By the middle of October, their bonds began to plummet and yields began to spike. Their unsecured debit was yielding 15%...everyone was confused for why a neocloud with $130B+ in backlog was seeing their debt get sold this aggressively. At the same time, Jensen went to Europe for business and back in the states, you couldn't go a day without some type of datacenter delay, credit headline, backstop issues...basically, the entire market started wondering if the financing of this buildout was possible. The 10 year hit 5.4%, the S&P stayed at all time highs, and AI stocks started to weaken but they didn't give out yet. You could've sold and protected some gains here across the entire market, but if you didn't, November was going to be what really wrecked you.

We enter November with the midterms. Everyone, including myself, though it was going to be a clearing event. Instead, it ended up being an event that showed the market that democrats had such a majority of support because of the concerns around the Iran war (which still hadn't ended) and datacenter backlash, that now what needed to be priced in was the slowdown of the buildout and a potential 2027 peak to capex growth.

This changed everything, and the market really started to feel it. By the middle of November, Jensen was ousted as CEO after reports about affairs with a Chinese spy and the market basically round tripped across the entire AI trade. The only safety during this time was consumer staples like $MCD $TGT $COST, basically companies that didn't have anything to do with AI. We got some horrible inflation reports so the chances for a hike went further up and that continued to put pressure on growth stocks. By last Friday, the S&P hit $689 as the Nasdaq fell 5.5% in a day and we wiped out $7.4T of marketcap within a week. 

We still don't know if that was the bottom or if we created a double bottom with Wednesday's price action and maybe we are out of the woods, but most AI names ended up either going negative YTD or meaningfully came down from their peak. 

All of this to say, it's been a hard year. I think everyone should have some empathy for everyone this year. If you were heavy on margin, chances are you got wiped out as we saw the KOSPI in South Korea round trip a +100% move on their entire index. If you didn't take profits at the top and just kept buying, even when the fundamentals made sense for a company like $MU when it was already down 30% from the highs, you had to experience another 25% decline. If you went short into the first ceasefire, you got hit hard. If you went long commodities at the end of Jan, you got hit hard. If you even picked SaaS names like $NOW at $80 and saw it go to $150 and didn't sell, you got hit hard because of one earnings. $META was a big winner for so many people as the company got through lawsuits and went from $520 to $780, but then they diluted and the stock crashed. Obviously, if you had a meaningful $NVDA position, you had to see that entire position go to 8x forward earnings because of what happened with Jensen. Crypto...didn't even really get to have a meaningful moment outside of the 60K to 85K pump on $BTC which gave some momentum to names like $MSTR $COIN and $HOOD but then Bitcoin also fell back below 60K and crypto ended up falling with tech stocks. 

I am not sure if 2027 is going to be this challenging or because we went through this year, maybe next year is going to be similar to one direction across all sectors.

What I do know is volatility is likely not going to end as this market has more and more narratives being part of the story daily with the Fed, AI's impact across the economy, geopolitics, and more. My fundamental belief is being long in exceptional companies that can compound earnings over the long term will likely outperform most strategies and there should be risk mitigation through trying to avoid the really excited moments or really ugly moments by never getting too happy or too sad. There's always opportunities to trim and opportunities to buy the dip, but being net long in the most important technology revolution we have ever seen is probably a better idea than not. 

Finally, I really think we should try to have more empathy for one another because the equity markets are supposed to be hard. We all follow them everyday because we are junkies that are obsessed with this game, but this game isn't easy, and 2026 showed how hard the game can be with all the things we had to navigate. Hoping 2027 is a little easier but even if it isn't, excited to still try to navigate and have a chance at playing the game.

Let's walk through how this year started and all of the things one needed to do in order to actually participate in the bull market...

To start off, I think 2026 was fundamentally different from 2023, 2024, and 2025 because of sector rotation and long/short pair trades across different sectors. 

Over the past 3 years, everyone lost money together across all industries when the markets went down and everyone made money when everything went up. The trend was quite literally your friend and if you followed it short, you won, if you followed it long, you won. 

2026 was different.

First, in January you had to basically get two trades right to really benefit: long oil and long metals. We saw gold and silver breakout of a 15 year base and we saw a Venezuela operation that made oil the most important commodity trade of the year. However, you then had to sell commodities into a blow off top by the end of January. If you didn't, you had a 40% drawdown waiting for you. 

As we got into the end of February, we saw the administration take us into a war. No one knew how long it really would last for as it was pitched as a short, special operation. It ended up taking the S&P down to 6200 and growth stocks were down 30-40%. Once again, you had to really be long oil or short the $QQQ to seriously benefit off of this.

So, let's say you bought the dip coming out of March and into April when the first ceasefire was announced. We essentially got the most aggressive, leveraged rally we had seen in a decade from March to June...but only in semis. 

If you didn't own the semis, you really didn't benefit. You also couldn't just own anything in $SMH, you had to own very high-beta semiconductor stocks that were the definition of picks and shovels, essentially the bottleneck bros trade. Owning $NVDA was not going to carry your year even though it was the most important semiconductor company. Now, you could have also participated in some other sectors, like space with names like $RKLB $RDW $ASTS, but you had to be aggressively in something within the most high-beta growth sectors for the market to feel comfortable giving you a premium. 

If you owned anything in software, you had to suffer 50-60% declines across some of the most incredible companies in the space like $PLTR, $SHOP, and $MSFT because the narrative became that Anthropic would kill software. $IGV got cut by 30%. 

Well, then comes July. Now, we finally figured out why software was getting hit as hard as it did. Leopold had made one trade very popular -- long semis, short software. Other hedgefunds had copied it. The problem was, the trade had become so popular and so leveraged that other market participants realized a collapse of the trade could literally wipe out entire funds and the overall sectors. As much money as was made on the upside for the AI trade, the downside had now begun. Leopold's fund blew up but survived, Citadel came in and bought everything at a steep discount, and AI names basically fell 50-60%. 

In August, we got a bounce. If the entire downside of the trade was based on a hedgefund getting over levered, then that meant the AI trade was back on since the main event had already taken place. However, things felt different. The excitement around memory had faded. The neoclouds were not seeing the same momentum as they were before. AI names were still doing well, but something obviously fell off. If you did not sell the June highs and chose to hold on, you were basically getting ready to roundtrip the entire gains as we progressed through the year. The space names literally fell 70% as $SPCX marked the top for the market and for the space names. 

The reason this is so important is because I believe many people bought most of these AI names in May/June, not early in the year. I am a victim of that as well. The rally was so aggressive that if you didn't have any meaningful semi exposure, you probably ended up buying something that was more rooted in hype even if the fundamentals were strong. I mean some of these names were flat for 25 years and had just seen a massive move up, so obviously there were a ton of people buying into names that likely were too high to begin with. 

Towards the end of August, the software trade finally started coming back, along with the hyperscalers. $META began showing off Muse, $MSFT guided to FCF positive, $AMZN had their best operating margins ever. Apple $AAPL was strong all year as a defensive play. The narrative about Claude destroying software went away. 

September was flat. Nothing crazy to see.

Then came October. We hit ATHs again, not every name in the AI trade got to their June highs, but many names came back. $NBIS was back to $250, $NVDA hit $240, it felt like the bull market was back in action. 

Unfortunately, $CRWV was the reason everything changed. By the middle of October, their bonds began to plummet and yields began to spike. Their unsecured debit was yielding 15%...everyone was confused for why a neocloud with $130B+ in backlog was seeing their debt get sold this aggressively. At the same time, Jensen went to Europe for business and back in the states, you couldn't go a day without some type of datacenter delay, credit headline, backstop issues...basically, the entire market started wondering if the financing of this buildout was possible. The 10 year hit 5.4%, the S&P stayed at all time highs, and AI stocks started to weaken but they didn't give out yet. You could've sold and protected some gains here across the entire market, but if you didn't, November was going to be what really wrecked you.

We enter November with the midterms. Everyone, including myself, though it was going to be a clearing event. Instead, it ended up being an event that showed the market that democrats had such a majority of support because of the concerns around the Iran war (which still hadn't ended) and datacenter backlash, that now what needed to be priced in was the slowdown of the buildout and a potential 2027 peak to capex growth.

This changed everything, and the market really started to feel it. By the middle of November, Jensen was ousted as CEO after reports about affairs with a Chinese spy and the market basically round tripped across the entire AI trade. The only safety during this time was consumer staples like $MCD $TGT $COST, basically companies that didn't have anything to do with AI. We got some horrible inflation reports so the chances for a hike went further up and that continued to put pressure on growth stocks. By last Friday, the S&P hit $689 as the Nasdaq fell 5.5% in a day and we wiped out $7.4T of marketcap within a week. 

We still don't know if that was the bottom or if we created a double bottom with Wednesday's price action and maybe we are out of the woods, but most AI names ended up either going negative YTD or meaningfully came down from their peak. 

All of this to say, it's been a hard year. I think everyone should have some empathy for everyone this year. If you were heavy on margin, chances are you got wiped out as we saw the KOSPI in South Korea round trip a +100% move on their entire index. If you didn't take profits at the top and just kept buying, even when the fundamentals made sense for a company like $MU when it was already down 30% from the highs, you had to experience another 25% decline. If you went short into the first ceasefire, you got hit hard. If you went long commodities at the end of Jan, you got hit hard. If you even picked SaaS names like $NOW at $80 and saw it go to $150 and didn't sell, you got hit hard because of one earnings. $META was a big winner for so many people as the company got through lawsuits and went from $520 to $780, but then they diluted and the stock crashed. Obviously, if you had a meaningful $NVDA position, you had to see that entire position go to 8x forward earnings because of what happened with Jensen. Crypto...didn't even really get to have a meaningful moment outside of the 60K to 85K pump on $BTC which gave some momentum to names like $MSTR $COIN and $HOOD but then Bitcoin also fell back below 60K and crypto ended up falling with tech stocks. 

I am not sure if 2027 is going to be this challenging or because we went through this year, maybe next year is going to be similar to one direction across all sectors.

What I do know is volatility is likely not going to end as this market has more and more narratives being part of the story daily with the Fed, AI's impact across the economy, geopolitics, and more. My fundamental belief is being long in exceptional companies that can compound earnings over the long term will likely outperform most strategies and there should be risk mitigation through trying to avoid the really excited moments or really ugly moments by never getting too happy or too sad. There's always opportunities to trim and opportunities to buy the dip, but being net long in the most important technology revolution we have ever seen is probably a better idea than not. 

Finally, I really think we should try to have more empathy for one another because the equity markets are supposed to be hard. We all follow them everyday because we are junkies that are obsessed with this game, but this game isn't easy, and 2026 showed how hard the game can be with all the things we had to navigate. Hoping 2027 is a little easier but even if it isn't, excited to still try to navigate and have a chance at playing the game.

It's been three weeks since this post. Many people, myself included, are incredibly interested in this report, and more specifically, in Anthropic's AL4 number. I'm Sam, one of Anthropic's co-founders, and I lead much of our safety work. I'm going to have more to share on that work over the coming months.

I thought I'd start by sharing a few thoughts on the latest report from @METR_Evals.

The speed of progress in model capabilities is one of the most important questions in AI safety, and METR’s work here provides the public with an independent, external view into how this is happening inside Anthropic. I’ll talk more about some of the details below, but first some context for those new to this work.

How quickly AI progress is accelerating has many important safety implications, since it determines how quickly the risks from advanced models increase. But, because most research happens within the frontier labs, it’s difficult for external observers and policy makers to get a strong sense of what that rate is. We kicked off the process with METR that led to this report earlier in the year, in anticipation of progress continuing to accelerate.

For this report, we gave METR access to a range of sensitive internal data, including benchmark scores for unreleased models, estimates of how models are progressing, and interviews with our researchers. They had complete independence to form their own conclusions.

Many of their conclusions match my own. AI is speeding up our research, but it’s hard to say exactly how much. While they conclude AI can't yet make the most important contributions to model training on its own, they think the pace of development could, by default, accelerate further.

This work began well before and is separate from the embedded third-party evaluators that are part of our commitment to pacing the frontier, but it’s a good illustration of why we think evaluators are a good idea. The more access reviewers have, the clearer a picture they can form of the situation and the better-positioned they are to highlight situations like this one.

We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work. But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster. That would make the risks METR is worried about worse. That’s a tradeoff. I think we made the right call, though we’re continuing to assess the pros and cons here.

In the coming weeks, we plan to share a report with our own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic, including where we stand against our Responsible Scaling Policy, plus new steps we’re taking to strengthen our safety and security practices as AI keeps improving quickly.
